source: Lawson (1979) Cognitive strategies in architectural design, Ergonomics 22(1)
finding: Founding experiment. Final-year architecture students and postgraduate science students arranged coloured blocks into a one-layer structure so the perimeter showed as much of a target colour as possible, under hidden rules. Scientists tried many block mixes fast to discover the rule structure first. Architects picked blocks to hit the colour target and swapped in the next best option when a choice failed. Lawson labelled the two styles problem-focused and solution-focused.
numbers: Counts and significance not found in the secondary sources I saw. Secondary sources say over 6000 possible arrangements existed.
limits: Original paper not opened. Only secondary summaries seen (search result text). Small student samples; the task is a well-defined puzzle, not a real brief.
agent_relevance: Models that jump to a solution to learn the rules are using the architect strategy. Our schema should treat early conjecture as a probe, not a commitment.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Cross restates Lawson: scientists tried to discover the structure of the problem; architects generated a sequence of high-scoring solutions until one proved acceptable. Lawson repeated the experiment with first-year science and architecture students and did NOT find the same difference. So the style grows with education and experience in designing.
numbers: Follow-up used first-year students of both disciplines (N not given in the review). No difference found.
quote: The scientists operated what might be called a problem-focusing strategy... architects by contrast adopted a solution-focusing strategy.
limits: Boundary condition: the effect is learned, not innate. Review gives no N. The null in first-years is the key replication-type result.
agent_relevance: Solution-first is a learned expert habit. A scaffold for a model should not assume novices (weak or small models) benefit from it.

source: Restrepo & Christiaans (2004) Problem structuring and information access in design (DTRS6)
finding: Restrepo and Christiaans summarise the explanations for problem versus solution focus. Lawson and Thomas and Carroll: learned with education. Lloyd and Scott: set by specific experience. Christiaans, Dorst, Christiaans and Restrepo: differences exist even in homogeneous groups, so it may be idiosyncratic. They note there is no direct evidence that the style is situational and call for longitudinal studies.
numbers: No new N for Lawson. Thomas and Carroll (1979) say designers will be designers even if they can be problem solvers.
quote: designers will be designers even if they can be problem solvers
limits: Three competing explanations (education, specific experience, personal idiosyncrasy) are not separated by any longitudinal study they know of.
agent_relevance: Solution-first may be a trait of the agent run, not only of expertise. Log which mode a given attempt used.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Lloyd and Scott (1994), protocol study of experienced engineering designers: more experienced designers used more generative reasoning; less experienced used more deductive reasoning. Designers with specific experience of the problem type approached it through solution conjectures. The variable that matters is specific experience of the problem type, not general experience.
numbers: Protocol study, N not given in the review.
quote: It is the variable of specific experience of the problem type that enables designers to adopt a conjectural approach to designing
limits: Observational; experience not randomised. Mostly engineers and senior-student architects.
agent_relevance: Solution-first is gated by familiarity with the problem class. For a novel task, lean problem-side first; for a familiar class, conjecture first.

source: Restrepo & Christiaans (2004) Problem structuring and information access in design (DTRS6)
finding: Christiaans and Restrepo (2001): senior design students with the same level of experience wrote the problem in their own words after reading the brief. Some used abstract relations and concepts (problem-oriented); others used physical objects (solution-oriented). This difference in early representations was replicated in a later study with senior and intermediate students (Restrepo and Christiaans 2003).
numbers: Two studies with senior students, then a replication with senior plus intermediate students. N not given in this chapter.
limits: Same education level still split, so experience does not fully explain it. Student samples.
agent_relevance: A cheap test: ask the model to restate the brief before acting and code whether the restatement is relational or object-based. That may predict its mode.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Christiaans and Dorst (1992) and Cross, Christiaans and Dorst (1994), junior and senior industrial design students: juniors gathered little information and solved a simple problem, unaware of many criteria. Seniors split in two. The more successful group asked less information, processed it at once, and set priorities early. The other group gathered much information as a substitute for design work. Information need was linked to inability to cope with uncertainty, not to level of education.
numbers: Protocol study of student industrial designers; N per group not given in the review.
quote: gathering data was sometimes just a substitute activity for actually doing any design work
limits: Quality was creativity judged on the solution; small student samples.
agent_relevance: Warns against endless information gathering. Supports a budget on problem scoping with a forced move to conjecture.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Atman et al. (1999), freshmen versus senior engineering students: freshmen who spent a large share of time defining the problem did not produce quality designs. For seniors, attention to problem scoping (more and wider information) gave better designs. Some freshmen got stuck in problem definition. Quality was also tied to rapid alternation between design steps (transitions).
numbers: Protocol analysis of engineering students; N for the 1999 paper not in this review (see a17 for the later 2007 sample sizes).
quote: those subjects who spent a large proportion of their time defining the problem did not produce quality designs.
limits: Same time share has opposite effect by experience: a boundary condition. Secondary report, original not opened.
agent_relevance: Scoping helps only with enough knowledge to scope well. A weak model that scopes at length may drift. Count steps, check progress.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Co-evolution: Cross and Dorst (1998) studied experienced industrial designers: they explore the problem space, find a partial structure, use it to partly structure the solution space, check implications, and feed this back. Kolodner and Wills (1996), senior engineering students: proposed solutions remind designers of issues, so problem and solution co-evolve. Solution conjectures are the tool for understanding the problem.
numbers: Protocol studies, N not given in the review.
quote: Proposed solutions often directly remind designers of issues to consider. The problem and solution co-evolve.
limits: Interpretation of protocols; coding choices matter.
agent_relevance: Maps to a loop: conjecture, read the failure, update the problem statement. G2 says revise from real output; a conjecture that runs gives real output.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Framing in experts: Lloyd and Scott (1995) found experienced architects had strong problem paradigms or guiding themes. Cross and Clayburn Cross (1998) found outstanding engineers used a strong guiding theme. Darke (1979) found outstanding architects used primary generators to set problem boundaries and solution goals. Goel and Pirolli (1992): problem structuring dominates early but recurs throughout the task. Schon: framing is not done in one burst at the start.
numbers: Interviews and protocols, small N of outstanding designers.
quote: In each protocol there comes a time when the designer makes a statement that summarises how he or she sees the problem
limits: Selected outstanding designers; survivorship possible.
agent_relevance: Expert conjecture is anchored by a one-line frame (primary generator). Store the frame in memory and revisit it only on a signal.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Valkenburg and Dorst (1998) compared a successful and an unsuccessful student industrial design team. The successful team used five different frames in sequence; the unsuccessful team used a single frame and spent much more time on naming problem features rather than developing solution concepts.
numbers: One team versus one team.
limits: N = 2 teams; cannot separate cause from outcome.
agent_relevance: Changing frames went with success; single-frame lock-in went with failure. Supports reframing on a signal (G1), not a schedule.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Opportunism versus structure. Guindon (1990): designers often deviate from top-down; problem specification and solution development interleave; deviations are natural for ill-structured problems and cost little. Ball and Ormerod (1995), expert electronics engineers: very few deviations from top-down breadth-first, only quick depth-first probes of a concept to test viability. They argue experts mix both modes.
numbers: Protocol studies of software and electronics designers; N not given in the review.
quote: Much of what has been described as opportunistic behavior sits comfortably within a structured top-down design framework
limits: Competing accounts: opportunism as normal (Guindon) versus structure with probes (Ball and Ormerod). Discipline differs.
agent_relevance: Design the loop as breadth-first with cheap depth-first probes. A probe is run and checked, then dropped or kept.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Modal shifts. Akin and Lin (1995), one experienced engineering designer: six of eight novel design decisions occurred while the subject alternated rapidly among drawing, examining and thinking. Cross et al. (1994) and Atman et al. (1999): more successful students alternated rapidly between activity modes.
numbers: 6 of 8 novel design decisions in triple-mode periods. Single-subject case.
quote: Six out of a total of eight times a novel design decision was made, we found the subject alternating between these three activity modes
limits: Correlation only. The authors avoid claiming cause. Single designer.
agent_relevance: Interleave generate, examine and reason steps in short cycles rather than long blocks. Count transitions as a progress signal.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Novice versus expert strategy. Novices are usually depth-first, experts top-down and breadth-first, but Cross says this is too simple. Standard expertise results (chess, physics) come from well-defined problems. Creative experts deliberately treat the task as ill-defined, so they treat problems as harder than novices do, and solve similar tasks from first principles rather than recalling earlier solutions. Depth-first lowers cognitive load; breadth-first lowers commitment.
numbers: No single N. A neuroimaging line is also cited: experts used more visuo-spatial regions, novices more verbal-abstract regions (study not named in the excerpt I read).
quote: creative experts will define the given task so that it is problematic
limits: Mixes protocol findings from several fields (writing, programming, design).
agent_relevance: Expert design is not simple efficiency: it re-opens the problem. Do not equate speed with quality; reopening the frame is allowed only on a signal.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter)
finding: Akin and Akin (1996) on creative insight: an experienced architect had the procedural knowledge to break out of a conventional frame of reference and specify a new one (medium, goal, procedures); the non-architect novice could generate only a conventional solution.
numbers: Two subjects (one architect, one non-architect).
limits: N = 2; a case contrast.
agent_relevance: Breaking a frame needs a new representation plus procedures, not just a new idea. Reframe operators must give a way to test the new frame.

source: Kavakli & Gero (2001) Strategic knowledge differences between an expert and a novice designer
finding: Conceptual design protocols from one expert and one novice. The expert's cognitive activity and productivity were almost three times the novice's. Expert processing stays within short-term memory limits, uses fewer processes and groups them differently. Authors credit strategic knowledge built with experience.
numbers: N = 2 (one expert, one novice); ratio about 3 times.
limits: Abstract page only; coding details not shown. Two subjects cannot give a population estimate.
agent_relevance: Expert advantage is organisation of actions, not more actions. Keep each step small and structured; avoid long mixed steps.

source: Kavakli & Gero (2002) The structure of concurrent cognitive actions: a case study on novice and expert designers, Design Studies 23(1)
finding: Case study. The expert's concurrent cognitive actions fell into clear categories; many of the novice's were hard to classify and split into several groups. Expert was about three times as active and productive.
numbers: N = 2; ratio about 3 times (from search-result summary).
limits: Seen only through search snippets, not the article. Cited by later papers as showing experts are better organised.
agent_relevance: Same as a15: structure beats volume.

source: Atman, Adams, Cardella, Turns, Mosborg & Saleem (2007) Engineering design processes: A comparison of students and expert practitioners, J Eng Educ 96(4)
finding: Nineteen experts from several engineering fields designed a playground aloud in a lab. Their process and solution quality were compared with earlier data from 26 freshmen and 24 seniors. Main differences between advanced engineers and students were problem scoping and information gathering.
numbers: 19 experts, 26 freshmen, 24 seniors (from abstract text in search results). The page I opened shows only citation and keywords: design expertise, design process, problem scoping, iteration.
limits: Full text not obtained; numbers beyond the sample sizes not read. Lab task, one problem.
agent_relevance: Key counterpoint to solution-first: experts scoped MORE than students. Conjecture-first and thorough scoping coexist in experts.

source: Purzer et al. (2008) Comparing design problem solving processes of product design and engineering student teams in the US and UK (ASEE 2008-1709)
finding: Four student teams: two UK senior product design teams (3 men; 2 men plus 2 women) and two US freshman engineering teams. Seniors drew at every stage and relied on internal knowledge; both senior teams spent most time scoping and generating alternatives and under 10 percent on project realisation. The senior mixed team spent 4 minutes defining the problem before ideas; the all-male team started alternatives right after reading the brief. The senior mixed team made 48 iterations between scoping and alternatives.
numbers: 4 teams; seniors had 30 minutes; 48 iterations for the senior mixed team; under 10 percent realisation.
limits: Four teams, case comparison, not statistics. Teams versus individuals confound. Different task conditions and cultures.
agent_relevance: Even among seniors the start differs (idea at once vs 4 minutes of scoping). Build a schema that tolerates both.

source: Purzer et al. (2008) background section (ASEE 2008-1709): earlier expert-novice findings
finding: Background: Atman and colleagues found expert engineers spent more time on problem scoping and gathered more outside information than students; experts monitored and planned their process. Resnick: experts reinterpret and simplify problems and use drawings before solving. Individual designers gathered more task information before searching for solutions, while a team in the Delft workshop produced alternatives earlier but stepped back to clarify the task more often.
numbers: No new numbers; summary of cited work.
limits: Secondary; the Delft team finding contradicts expert-individual results, as the authors note.
agent_relevance: Multi-sample or team setups may shift timing toward early alternatives with later clarification; relevant to ensembles.

source: Morozov et al. (2007) Breadth in design problem scoping: using insights from experts to investigate student processes (ASEE 2007-1505)
finding: Midwest Floods retaining wall task. Four experts thought aloud (up to 30 minutes; none used all of it) versus 124 first-year students who wrote lists in 10 minutes. Novices gave 11.5 statements on average, experts 57. Novices gave more natural and social frames of reference (30 percent natural versus 18 percent for experts), a broader but less technical scope. Two of four experts showed a top-down, breadth-first approach.
numbers: n = 4 experts, n = 124 freshmen; 1418 novice statements; coder agreement 77 percent first pass, 72 percent average; expert design detail 30 to 51 percent versus context 49 to 70 percent.
limits: Different collection method (spoken versus written) blocks direct comparison; only 4 experts; one problem.
agent_relevance: Breadth in scope is not expert scoping: novices sounded broad but non-technical. Check the quality of frames, not only the count.

source: Atman, Turns, Cardella & Adams (2003) The design processes of engineering educators: thick descriptions (DTRS6)
finding: Design processes of engineering educators designing a playground vary a lot. In the table, the share of time on problem scoping runs from about 10 percent to about 30 percent, and on generating ideas from about 5 percent to about 66 percent across participants. Two participants stopped before detailed design; two stopped only after detailed design. Authors announce a follow-on with about 24 experts.
numbers: Seven participant columns of time and percent shares; total times between about 1 hr and 2.5 hr.
limits: Educators, not practising experts; column labelling not fully verified; no quality scores.
agent_relevance: Individual variation among experts is large. Do not tune the scaffold to one average expert profile.

source: Perisic, Martinec, Storga & Gero (2019) A computational study of the effect of experience on problem/solution space exploration in teams (ICED19)
finding: Agent-based model: agents hold part of a function-behaviour-structure knowledge graph, pass activation across weighted links, learn links, and share ideas with trust. 250 experiments, four tasks each; experienced teams kept learning, novices reset every task. Experts needed fewer steps and, per step, made more new structures and links, so they spent more of their effort on the solution side. Both hypotheses were supported.
numbers: Steps experts vs novices: task 1 290.7 vs 379.6; task 2 310.6 vs 401.5; task 3 316.2 vs 494.7 (p about 0.001 or below). New structures per step: 0.14 vs 0.09, 0.17 vs 0.08, 0.26 vs 0.09. New links per step: 1.07 vs 0.55, 1.19 vs 0.55, 1.32 vs 0.47.
limits: Results follow from design: experience is stored links, so the model shows what the theory assumes, not independent evidence. Raw counts of new links and structures were not significant on tasks 2 and 3 (p 0.178 to 0.97). Teams, not individuals.
agent_relevance: A computational account: solution-first follows from stored chunks that make solution nodes reachable at once. Memory of solved cases is the mechanism, which fits our memory goal.

source: Perisic et al. (2019) theory section: cited accounts of why experts go solution-first
finding: Accounts cited: experts store larger organised chunks and many solution examples (Petre 2004); Cross (2004): experts store and access larger cognitive chunks and recognise underlying principles rather than surface features; Liikkanen and Perttula (2009): novices start from problem structure if they cannot recognise a solution, experts recall more complex solutions without much decomposition; Ahmed et al. (2003): novices use trial and error, experienced designers use particular strategies; McComb et al. (2015): high-performing teams pick a good direction quickly with low divergence.
numbers: Cited findings, no new numbers.
quote: able to store and access information in larger cognitive `chunks' than novices can
limits: Secondary reading of other papers; I did not open Cross 2004, Ahmed 2003 or Liikkanen 2009.
agent_relevance: Chunked case memory gives immediate conjectures. Retrieval from stored solved cases is the cheapest route to expert-like solution-first behaviour.

source: Shin et al. (2025) No evidence for LLMs being useful in problem reframing (CHI 25)
finding: Between-subjects test with GPT-4o: manual reframing, direct LLM generation, free-form LLM use, and a structured approach from reframing theory. LLM use did not raise novelty or usefulness of problem frames as rated by 15 expert designers. Felt agency and ownership did not drop overall. Participants with more reframing knowledge (3 or more quiz items correct) made more novel frames with LLMs and felt more agency than novices, so LLM use widened the expert-novice gap.
numbers: 280 analysed participants (456 recruited, rest dropped); 4 conditions; 15 expert raters; August 2024 model; about 2 frames in 23.25 minutes per participant.
limits: Expertise measured by a short quiz, not years. Frame text only, no solution outcome. One model version. I did not extract exact test values beyond the nulls.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a generator model does not add problem-frame quality for designers. Use code-checked novelty rather than trusting the model.

source: Gold-affiliated authors (2024) Empirical study of problem-solution co-evolution in human-GAI collaboration (DRS 2024)
finding: Retrospective protocol study of twenty novice design students (13 women, 7 men, mean age 24) in four groups of five: three using ChatGPT, Midjourney or both, and a control. Coded abductive reasoning in problem-solution co-evolution; 40 conceptual designs rated for creativity. Some AI groups showed more abductive reasoning than control (7.2 units at the 10 percent level for one group) and abductive reasoning raised creativity scores.
numbers: N = 20, 5 per group; 40 designs; coder agreement checked on about 10 percent of data; effects at 1 to 10 percent significance levels.
limits: Very small N, novices only, no expert group, lenient 10 percent level.
agent_relevance: Suggests generative tools shift novice design toward solution-side abductive moves; weak evidence, test before relying on it.

source: Jackson, Cha, Prikladnicki & van der Hoek (2026) The role of LLMs in collaborative software design (FSE Companion 26)
finding: Eighteen pairs of software professionals (36 people, some with only 1 year of experience) designed a bicycle parking app in 90 minutes with a ChatGPT-based chat tool. Four usage modes: non-use, information source, producer, generator. Pairs used the LLM to explore both problem and solution space. Teams rarely accepted output as is; they scrutinised it, compared it with the brief and their design, and cherry-picked parts, treating output as a straw man.
numbers: 18 pairs, 36 participants, 90 minutes; 25 had used an LLM at work.
limits: Exploratory, qualitative, one greenfield task; no quality measurement or controlled novice versus expert split.
agent_relevance: LLM output is used as a conjecture to attack, which matches solution-first. Our scaffold should treat model output as a draft to be tested.

source: Gong et al. (2026) How LLM-based agents shape engineering design thinking: a qualitative study with software engineering students (ASEE 2026)
finding: Semester course, 40 students in eight teams. LLM agents took over retrieval and code generation. Design shifted from ideate-prototype-test to a fast prompt-evaluate-refine loop. Two strategies appeared: using output as inspiration versus delegating. Cognitive load moved to upstream problem scoping and downstream evaluation. The agents raised the performance floor.
numbers: 40 participants, 8 teams; qualitative.
limits: Qualitative, one course, one institution; no controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: The loop is solution-first by default (prompt yields a draft, then evaluate). The skill left to humans is scoping and checking, which a scaffold should supply.

source: Lim, Choi & Hong (2024) Identify design problems through questioning: role-playing with LLMs (CSCW Companion 24)
finding: Design novices find problem identification hard and tend to accept instructor feedback passively. A ChatGPT role-play probe lets students ask questions to identify problems. Sixteen students wrote 172 inputs, 10.8 per student on average (SD 4.5), about 13.6 words each (SD 10.4).
numbers: 16 students, 172 inputs.
limits: Preliminary probe, no control, no outcome measure.
agent_relevance: Novices can be moved toward problem questions by a role-play partner; an agent could use a questioning mode to test frames.

source: Cross (2001) Design cognition: results from protocol and other empirical studies of design activity (review chapter) (section 3: solution generation)
finding: Cross argues the solution-focused habit suits ill-defined problems that cannot become well-defined, so designers satisfice instead of optimise. A drawback is fixation by existing solutions. Cross concludes conventional expertise wisdom is often contradicted by expert designers and that we lack a good account of what makes design expertise.
numbers: Conceptual; no numbers.
limits: 2001 review; later work (Atman 2007) shows experts also scope more.
agent_relevance: Allow solution-first when the problem is ill-defined; add a fixation check when a prior solution is at hand.
